newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Japanese eaters in hot dog contest.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Japanese eaters in hot dog contest.

text.p: This is one contest where biting is allowed.

Just days after Mike Tyson was disqualified for sinking his teeth into the ears of world boxing champion Evander Holyfield, two champion hot dog eaters "weighed in" on Thursday at a boxing-style news conference outside City Hall.

World hot dog eating champion Hirofumi Nakajima of Japan and his American challenger Ed "The Animal" Krachie stared each other down in preparation for their re-match at the Fourth of July Hot Dog Contest at Coney Island in Brooklyn.

The 6-foot-6-inch (1.9 metre) American towered over his slim rival. It was their first meeting since November when Nakajima set a world record by chewing and swallowing 23 1/4 hot dogs in 12 minutes, almost two more than his opponent.
"I've been eating a lot, working on my technique a little," said the 330-pound (150 kg) New Yorker, who vowed revenge. "I'll have a heart attack, or I'll have a stroke, or I'm coming out on top."
Nakajima, a 22-year-old furniture delivery worker from Kofu, Japan, showed off the rhinestone-studded Mustard Yellow International Belt and trophy he won last year.
"I just like to eat, I don't really know how I manage to eat so much," the 135-pound (61 kg) Nakajima said through an interpreter. "Ed said he was going to eat 25 hot dogs, so I'm going to eat 26."

Nakajima became Japan's eating champion before competing against Krachie. He ate 15 bowls of noodle soup, 100 pieces of sushi, five plates of wheat noodles, five plates of beef over rice and five plates of curry over rice.
The hot dog contest has been held at Nathan's Famous restaurant in Coney Island each year since 1916, when Nathan Handwerker borrowed $320 to open his hot dog restaurant.
Nakajima and Krachie will be joined at a long table in the restaurant by 18 other competitive eaters from Japan and the United States, the contest's promoters said.
Hot dogs are popular, particularly on Independence Day. The National Hot Dog Council estimates that Americans will eat 88 million at July 4 picnics and 7 billion over the summer.
